title: Jota wins rain-shortened Silverstone opener
dek: Oliver Turvey and Simon Dolan won the rain-shortened 3 Hours of Silverstone for Jota Sport from pole, after a Safety Car lottery shuffled the LMP2 leaders.

chapters.title: A new-look series opens in the wet
text: The 3 Hours of Silverstone on 13 April 2013 opened a European Le Mans Series that had been rebuilt after a thin 2012. Races were cut from six hours to three, meetings shrank to two days and ran as support to other championships, and the WEC's Gerard Neveu took overall charge of the series. The class structure was simplified to LMP2 at the top, a single GTE class, the one-make Oreca FLM09 LMPC cars and GTC for GT3 machinery. Silverstone was a joint weekend with the opening round of the FIA World Endurance Championship, and the ELMS race served as its curtain raiser. A five-round calendar followed, running through Imola, the Red Bull Ring and the Hungaroring to a finale at Paul Ricard.

LMP2 was the story of the grid. Jota Sport arrived with Simon Dolan and a new Pro team-mate in Oliver Turvey, who was making his LMP2 debut in the Nissan-powered Zytek Z11SN. Thiriet by TDS Racing came as reigning champions, now carrying the number 1 and pairing Pierre Thiriet with Jonathan Hirschi. Signatech Alpine returned a famous French name to endurance racing in a rebadged Oreca, the only full-season LMP2 on Michelin tyres, with Pierre Ragues and Nelson Panciatici. Murphy Prototypes ran Brendon Hartley and Mark Patterson, while Morand Racing brought a Morgan for Natacha Gachnang and Frank Mailleux. Greaves Motorsport entered Chris Dyson and Michael Marsal in its #3 Zytek, and the pair were doubling up with the same team's WEC entry that weekend.

The weather made preparation almost meaningless. The first practice session started on a soaked, aquaplaning Silverstone, with spins into the gravel the order of the morning. In the afternoon Turvey set the pace on 1:51.699, with the Alpine and the Morgan close behind, as the cars moved from wets to slicks late in the session.

chapters.title: Turvey takes pole by eight tenths
text: Qualifying was held in a drying Silverstone, with the prototypes running in a separate twenty-minute session after the GT cars. The track was still greasy early on, and several drivers spun while looking for grip. Panciatici first put the Alpine on provisional pole, ahead of Niederhauser in the Race Performance Oreca, before Turvey took over in the final minutes.

Turvey went through 1:48.463 and 1:48.060 before settling on 1:48.032, and the Jota Zytek was on pole by roughly eight tenths of a second. He later said that all three of his quick laps would have been good enough for the top spot, and that he would start the race himself, with the drivers planning to split the distance evenly. Hartley's Murphy Oreca was second on 1:48.863, although the New Zealander never found a clear lap in traffic and parked the car in the pits with a couple of minutes left. Panciatici was third for Signatech Alpine on 1:49.063.

Niederhauser was fourth on 1:50.010 for Race Performance, followed by Mailleux's Morgan on 1:50.139 and Hirschi's Thiriet Oreca on 1:50.157, so six different teams filled the first three rows. Bastien Brière was seventh for Boutsen Ginion on 1:52.072, ahead of Dyson's Greaves Zytek on 1:52.529.

chapters.title: Chaos on slicks, five leaders in an hour
text: The rain arrived just as the cars reached the grid, and almost everyone started on slicks. A spinning LMPC car hit the pit wall right in front of the field as the lights went green, and the first corners were littered with spinners. The pit lane was halfway round the lap, so the quickest thinkers dived in for full wets before the Safety Car came out. Under the new series regulation the pit lane then stayed closed for the first three laps behind it, and everyone who had stayed out on slicks paid heavily. Turvey, the pole-sitter, slipped to seventh on the opening lap and Dyson lost a stack of places after a spin.

Mailleux was the beneficiary at the restart, until Hartley, who had made the tyre change in time, came through the field and took the lead around the outside at Stowe about 24 minutes in with a succession of fastest laps. He then ran wide at Stowe and beached the Oreca in the gravel, handing the lead back to Mailleux, who within minutes aquaplaned at Hangar Straight and put the Morgan backwards into the tyre wall. Panciatici spun the Alpine across country and conceded second to Hirschi, then third to Turvey, who had recovered to fifth. By the hour mark Turvey was leading again, before Dolan took over and clipped the barrier at Vale with only superficial damage.

chapters.title: Safety Car and a pit stop lottery
text: The second hour belonged to Thiriet by TDS. Hirschi moved to the front and the reigning champions held the lead as the race neared its midpoint. Then the conditions worsened so badly that the Safety Car came out again and stayed on track for nearly 50 minutes. Cars were still sliding off behind it, and Murphy Prototypes lost several laps in a long stop.

The Safety Car was decisive in the pit stops. TDS brought the lead car in for a driver change to Thiriet, and Jota, running with the benefit of strategy, was in front again after the leaders had stopped. Jota's Zytek stayed in front under the Safety Car until the weather made any resumption unrealistic.

chapters.title: Race stopped after 48 laps
text: With the rain refusing to ease, the race was brought to an early finish after 48 laps, 75 per cent of the scheduled three hours, with the official running time standing at 2:15:22. Jota Sport won the season opener, with Dolan and Turvey leading home Race Performance's Oreca-Judd of Michel Frey and Patric Niederhauser by 4.619 seconds on the same lap. Pierre Thiriet and Jonathan Hirschi completed the podium in the Thiriet by TDS Oreca, 5.485 seconds off the winner.

Signatech Alpine's Ragues and Panciatici were fourth, also on the lead lap, after a spin in the first hour had cost Panciatici second place. The remaining classified LMP2 cars were well adrift. Boutsen Ginion was 11th, two laps down, and the DKR Engineering Lola 15th, five laps back. Murphy Prototypes was classified 18th, seven laps behind after its long stop. Greaves and Morand did not make the classification.

chapters.title: A win built on a pole and a strategy
text: For Jota it was the perfect start to a new partnership. Turvey called it a great first weekend in LMP2 and the European Le Mans Series, with pole and a race win in very tricky conditions, and said that slipping to seventh on the first lap had been a hard moment. Team principal Sam Hignett said the pairing had worked well, with Turvey mighty in qualifying and Dolan managing extremely well in dreadful conditions, and added that on pure pace he believed the team were worthy winners, even if they would have liked to fight to the chequered flag. The winning Zytek Z11SN was powered by a Nissan engine built and serviced by Zytek.

Hartley took the blame for the gravel. He said he had made a massive error of judgement by braking too late in changing conditions and was kicking himself, having been fast on the wet tyres. Dyson called it a rough way to return to racing in Europe, with standing water and driving rain making staying on the track partly a matter of luck.

For the rest of the LMP2 field the day was a lesson in how quickly a lead could vanish: Murphy Prototypes had led with Hartley and Morand Racing with Mailleux, yet neither reached the finish in contention.
The ELMS now travels to Imola in Italy for round two on 18 May.

facts.v: Heavy rain ended the race after 48 laps, 75 per cent of the three-hour distance, with an official duration of 2:15:22.

one.label: Motorsport.com: Home triumph for Jota Sport in the wet at Silverstone

facts.v: A new series rule kept the pit lane shut for the first three laps of a Safety Car period, which cost the cars that had stayed on slicks.
Oliver Turvey took pole with 1:48.032, roughly eight tenths clear of the rest, on his LMP2 debut.
After qualifying the stewards relegated the Greaves Zytek to the back of the grid for a tyre-regulation infringement.
Having completed 75 per cent of the distance, the race paid full points.
